notes.front: What is the central goal that Team Topologies is optimizing organizations for?
notes.back: Fast flow of change — the ability to deliver value to customers quickly, safely, and sustainably, by removing hand-offs and organizational friction.

notes.front: What is Conway's Law?
notes.back: Organizations design systems that mirror their own communication structure. Coined by Melvin Conway in 1968.

notes.front: What is the 'Reverse Conway Maneuver'?
notes.back: Deliberately evolving a team and organizational structure first, so that the desired software architecture emerges as a natural consequence of the new communication paths.

notes.front: Why does Team Topologies treat the team, not the individual, as the fundamental means of software delivery?
notes.back: Because complex software delivery requires more skill and context than one person can hold; a long-lived, stable team is the smallest effective unit for that work.

notes.front: What is a 'team-first' approach in Team Topologies?
notes.back: Prioritizing the long-term health, cognitive load, and purpose of the team over individual role optimization or short-term task assignment.

notes.front: Team Topologies recommends teams remain stable for how long, and why?
notes.back: Long-lived (often years), because team stability builds trust, shared context, and delivery velocity that gets reset every time a team is reformed.

notes.front: What does Team Topologies say about the 'ideal' team size, referencing Dunbar's number?
notes.back: Roughly 5-9 people (a 'two-pizza team'), small enough to stay within a trusted, low-communication-overhead group.

notes.front: What is a 'Team API' in Team Topologies?
notes.back: The combination of a team's code, versioned interfaces, documentation, wiki, communication channels, and practices — everything other teams need to interact with it.

notes.front: What is 'cognitive load' in the Team Topologies sense?
notes.back: The total amount of mental effort a team needs to expend to do its work effectively — the basis for deciding how much responsibility a team can own.

notes.front: Name the three types of cognitive load defined by Team Topologies (from cognitive psychology).
notes.back: Intrinsic, extraneous, and germane cognitive load.

notes.front: Define intrinsic cognitive load.
notes.back: The inherent difficulty of the task itself — e.g. the fundamental complexity of the business domain or algorithm being worked on.

notes.front: Define extraneous cognitive load.
notes.back: Effort wasted on the environment in which the task is done — e.g. bad tooling, poor documentation, or unreliable deployment pipelines. This should be minimized.

notes.front: Define germane cognitive load.
notes.back: Effort needed for the specific aspects of the task that require special attention or care, such as learning or improving the domain model.

notes.front: Why does Team Topologies say software domains should be sized to fit team cognitive load, rather than the reverse?
notes.back: Because assigning a team more domain than it can hold in its head degrades quality, slows delivery, and burns people out; the domain boundary should match what a team can reliably own.

notes.front: List the four fundamental team types in Team Topologies.
notes.back: Stream-aligned team, enabling team, complicated-subsystem team, platform team.

notes.front: What is a stream-aligned team?
notes.back: A team aligned to a single, valuable stream of work (e.g. a product, service, user journey, or persona) that can deliver value directly to the customer, end to end.

notes.front: In Team Topologies, why is the stream-aligned team considered the 'primary' team type?
notes.back: Because it is the type through which value actually flows to the customer; the other three team types exist to reduce the cognitive load of stream-aligned teams.

notes.front: What is an enabling team?
notes.back: A team of specialists in a given technical or product domain that helps stream-aligned teams overcome gaps in knowledge, typically for a limited period, without taking over the work.

notes.front: What is the primary purpose of an enabling team, and what should it avoid becoming?
notes.back: To increase the autonomy and capability of stream-aligned teams by transferring skills; it should avoid becoming a permanent dependency or bottleneck.

notes.front: What is a complicated-subsystem team?
notes.back: A team responsible for a part of the system that requires deep specialist knowledge (e.g. a math-heavy video codec or trading algorithm), reducing the cognitive load stream-aligned teams would otherwise carry.

notes.front: When is it appropriate to form a complicated-subsystem team, according to Team Topologies?
notes.back: Only when a subsystem genuinely requires specialist expertise that most team members could not reasonably acquire, and only if the cognitive load reduction is worth the coordination cost.

notes.front: What is a platform team?
notes.back: A team that provides internal services (a 'platform') to reduce the cognitive load of stream-aligned teams, letting them deliver work with substantial autonomy via self-service APIs and tools.

notes.front: What is the definition of a 'platform' according to Team Topologies?
notes.back: A foundation of self-service APIs, tools, services, knowledge, and support that is arranged as a compelling internal product, enabling teams to deliver value with reduced cognitive load and coordination.

notes.front: Why does Team Topologies caution against calling every shared internal team a 'platform team'?
notes.back: Because the label implies a self-service, product-like offering with clear APIs; teams that merely centralize work without a self-service interface create hand-offs rather than reducing cognitive load.

notes.front: What is a 'thinnest viable platform' (TVP)?
notes.back: The smallest, simplest possible internal platform that meets the current needs of stream-aligned teams — avoiding over-engineering a platform ahead of actual demand.

notes.front: What new organizational concept does the 2nd edition of Team Topologies introduce for platform teams?
notes.back: The 'platform grouping' — a platform team can now consist of one or more teams grouped together under a shared mission, rather than always being a single team.

notes.front: In the 2nd edition's 'platform grouping' concept, what collaborates within a single grouping?
notes.back: Different team types and sub-groupings collaborate toward the same shared goal within the grouping, rather than each team acting in isolation.

notes.front: Besides the platform grouping concept, what other major additions does the Team Topologies 2nd edition make?
notes.back: Ten new case studies from organizations worldwide, plus a new foreword and afterword from the authors reflecting on the book's impact and future direction.

notes.front: List the three fundamental team interaction modes in Team Topologies.
notes.back: Collaboration, X-as-a-Service, and facilitating.

notes.front: Describe the 'collaboration' interaction mode.
notes.back: Two teams work closely together for a defined period, sharing responsibility and discovering new approaches together — high communication, but also high cognitive load for both teams.

notes.front: When should the 'collaboration' interaction mode be used, and why should it be time-boxed?
notes.back: During discovery or when rapid learning across a boundary is needed; it should be time-boxed because sustained collaboration increases cognitive load and blurs team responsibility.

notes.front: Describe the 'X-as-a-Service' interaction mode.
notes.back: One team consumes something (an API, tool, or service) provided by another team with minimal collaboration — clear ownership, low cognitive load, but less flexibility.

notes.front: Describe the 'facilitating' interaction mode.
notes.back: One team (typically an enabling team) helps another team learn or adopt something new, clearing obstacles, without doing the work for them.

notes.front: Which interaction mode is typical between a stream-aligned team and a platform team in steady state?
notes.back: X-as-a-Service — the stream-aligned team consumes the platform's self-service capabilities with minimal ongoing collaboration.

notes.front: Which interaction mode is typical between an enabling team and a stream-aligned team?
notes.back: Facilitating — the enabling team helps build capability in the stream-aligned team, then steps back.

notes.front: Why does Team Topologies insist that a team should only use one interaction mode with another team at a time?
notes.back: Because mixing modes (e.g. simultaneously collaborating and providing X-as-a-Service) creates unclear expectations and hidden hand-offs, undermining the purpose of naming the interaction explicitly.

notes.front: What does it mean to 'sense' organizational and technical needs in Team Topologies?
notes.back: Continuously observing signals — like cognitive overload, communication bottlenecks, or slow flow — and using them as feedback to evolve team boundaries and interactions over time.

notes.front: According to Team Topologies, what should trigger a change in team topology?
notes.back: Evidence of friction: excessive cognitive load, slow flow of change, repeated hand-offs, or misalignment between the team structure and the value stream — not a fixed schedule.

notes.front: What is meant by an 'evolutionary' approach to team topologies?
notes.back: Team structures and interaction modes are not fixed; organizations should expect and plan for them to change incrementally as products, technology, and understanding evolve.

notes.front: What is a common anti-pattern where teams keep collaborating in a mode they should have moved on from?
notes.back: Getting 'stuck' in the collaboration mode long after the shared learning it was meant to produce has already happened, inflating cognitive load unnecessarily.

notes.front: What warning does Team Topologies give about organizations that never change their team structures?
notes.back: Static team structures tend to fall out of alignment with the software architecture and value streams, reintroducing hand-offs and slow flow over time.

notes.front: What is a 'value stream' in the Team Topologies sense?
notes.back: The sequence of activities an organization undertakes to deliver value to a customer, from initial concept through to running software in the hands of users.

notes.front: Why does Team Topologies emphasize fracture planes / boundaries when splitting systems between teams?
notes.back: Because splitting a system along natural fracture planes (e.g. bounded contexts, compliance boundaries, risk boundaries) keeps each team's part loosely coupled, reducing hand-offs and shared cognitive load.

notes.front: Name two examples of 'fracture planes' Team Topologies suggests for splitting software systems between teams.
notes.back: Any two of: business domain bounded context, regulatory/compliance boundary, change-cadence boundary, risk boundary, performance-isolation boundary, user-persona boundary, technology boundary.

notes.front: How does Team Topologies relate to Domain-Driven Design's 'bounded context'?
notes.back: A bounded context is one of the recommended fracture planes for aligning a stream-aligned team's ownership boundary with a coherent part of the business domain.
